title: Woodenization
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Named for UCLA coach John Wooden's famous practice of teaching players to tie their shoes, Woodenization is Stuart's seventh Will to Learn strategy: explicitly and clearly teaching every learning-conducive behavior a teacher expects, rather than assuming students already know how to do it. He distinguishes Smallies from Biggies, and argues the most common teacher error is misjudging a Biggie as a Smallie. He closes by reframing Woodenization not as an added burden but as a long-run time-saver, since front-loaded instruction prevents the recurring cleanup work of unmet expectations.
points: The Smallies/Biggies distinction is Stuart's key diagnostic tool: Smallies need only a brief mini-lesson and reinforcement, while Biggies require sustained instruction, examples, and non-examples.
He argues teachers most often err by misclassifying a Biggie as a Smallie, overestimating what secondary students should already be able to do consistently.
Stuart flags learning-styles theory as a specific example of a widely taught but empirically uncorroborated method that shouldn't be Woodenized into classroom practice.
He reframes the apparent extra workload of Woodenization as a net time-saver, arguing it prevents the much larger recurring cost of remedying situations that never needed to arise.
quotes: The gist is this: For any learning-conducive behavior you want your students to do, clearly and effectively teach them how to do that thing well.
What's remarkable in the quotation above is how lengthy it is. Wooden put a great deal of thought into what effective shoe-tying looked like, and he brought that clarity to his players.

The most common error teachers make is mis-categorizing a Biggie as a Smallie. Us secondary teachers can be pretty misguided at judging what students should be able to do with 100% consistency and proficiency by the time they reach us.
Despite decades of studies, learning style theory has yet to be empirically corroborated. Because of this, I do not recommend teaching learning style theory to students.
How much time have you spent in your career remedying situations that would have never arisen had students just done the things you asked them to do?
I know what I'm doing. I care about your success. I'll leave nothing to chance. And on this team, our efforts will pay off — you can count on it.
